title: Just one thing
hook: abandon greed, just that one thing, and I guarantee the fruit

segments.voice: Yesterday: Khujjuttara and the flower money, and your line, thus it was said. Did you pass on something you were once told? Today, the very first teaching in her book. Day six hundred twenty-seven.

Self-help shelves are full of lists. Seven habits. Twelve rules. Thirty days to a better you. Lists are useful, and the Buddhist texts love them too: four truths, eight factors, five hindrances. But sometimes a list is a way of putting things off; there's always one more item to read about before starting. The Itivuttaka opens with no list at all. Its section of ones begins with a single thing, and an unusual promise. The Buddha doesn't say try this. He says: I guarantee it. Today: just one thing.
screen: `SEVEN HABITS, TWELVE RULES.` → `A LIST CAN BE A DELAY.` → `ONE THING, AND A GUARANTEE.`

segments.voice: Here is the first teaching of the book, after the opening line, this was said by the Blessed One, so I heard. Abandon one thing, monks, and I am your guarantee of non-return. What one thing? Greed. Non-return is a technical term. In the early texts, it's the third of four stages of awakening: someone who has gone so far that they won't be reborn in this world of the senses again. So the promise is enormous. And the condition is one thing. The verse that follows explains: driven by greed, beings go to a bad destination; seeing greed rightly, those who understand let it go, and having let it go, they don't come back to this world. Then the very next teachings say the same, one at a time. Abandon one thing: hatred. Then: delusion. Then anger, then contempt, then conceit. Each one, alone, with the same guarantee. Why would one be enough? The text doesn't say. One way teachers explain it: these aren't six separate weeds; pull one up by the root, really by the root, and the others turn out to grow from the same soil. Notice the word guarantee, too. The Pali word, patibhoga, means a guarantor, someone who stands surety. In the text, the Buddha puts his own word behind the promise.
screen: `ABANDON ONE THING: GREED.` · `NON-RETURN, THE THIRD STAGE.` · `HATRED, DELUSION, ANGER, CONCEIT.` · `I STAND AS YOUR GUARANTEE.` · then, large: `JUST ONE THING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: abandon one small thing. Sit and settle. Ask, where does a little greed show up in my day? A second helping you don't want. Checking a price again. Wanting the last word. Choose just one, and make it small. Picture the moment it usually happens, and picture yourself letting it go: hand open, breath out. Not forever. Just today. The bell holds the time.
Just one thing. The opening of the Itivuttaka: abandon greed, just that, and the Buddha stands as your guarantee. Today's word.
Your line: just one thing. Today, don't fix everything. Let go of the one small grab you chose, once, and notice what's left. Day six hundred twenty-seven.

screen: `DAY 627 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SHARE EVEN THE LAST BITE.`

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often name greed, hatred and delusion as the three roots of unwholesome action, and some practitioners work with one of them at a time.

match.prompt: just one thing: tap the pairs.

myth: the Itivuttaka opens with a long list of rules
it opens with one thing: abandon greed.
the Buddha says 'I am your guarantee' of non-return
he puts himself on the line for the one who lets go of greed.
the same promise is made for hatred and delusion, one at a time
the next teachings repeat it for hatred, delusion, anger, contempt and conceit.

fork.setup: you want to make real progress on the path. the Itivuttaka's first teaching offers a deal. what is it?
options: master eight things and you might succeed.
abandon just greed, and the Buddha guarantees non-return.
fork.reveal: one thing, and a guarantee. the same offer follows for hatred, delusion, anger, contempt and conceit.

original.note: Pali lobha: greed, the one thing to abandon in Itivuttaka 1, first of the three unwholesome roots.

trapdoor: what you thought: real change takes a long list of rules.
what it means: the Itivuttaka says let go of one root, greed, fully, and the Buddha himself guarantees the result.
what a scholar hears: Iti 1–6 use the formula 'ekadhammam pajahatha, aham vo patibhogo anagamitaya', patibhogo being a surety or guarantor.

sources.ref: Itivuttaka 1–6 (Lobha, Dosa, Moha, Kodha, Makkha, Mana Suttas)

notes: Itivuttaka 1 paraphrased. Confirm the sequence of Iti 1–6 (greed, hatred, delusion, anger, contempt, conceit).
Confirm patibhogo as 'surety, guarantor' and the gloss of non-return (anagami) as the third stage.
The 'same soil' explanation is the writer's illustration, not the text's.

Editor review (y2 614-631): the review claimed Iti 1 was the first teaching Khujjuttara carried home (no source says so); now 'the first teaching in her book'. The 'same soil' explanation is now marked as one teachers' explanation rather than narrator fact; trimmed the surety gloss ('for a loan') and the narrator's 'not how a teacher talks if he isn't sure'; 'many practitioners' softened.
